subject: mqmautocofactors() outputs different sets of cofactors, hence different LOD scores, on different runs

messages.author: 9ddf1f5ad51e8c4f
messages.subject: mqmautocofactors() outputs different sets of cofactors, hence different LOD scores, on different runs
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to use MQM mapping on a RIL population of 178 lines with 1221 markers. On average my markers are about 1 cM apart.

I used mqmautocofactors() to select a set of 158 markers to be the cofactors. The number 158 comes from the number of lines minus 20.

cofactors <- mqmautocofactors(mycross, num = nind(mydata1.argmax)-20, distance = 1, verbose = T)

The function outputs different sets of 158 cofactors every time I run the function. Here are 4 examples.

And when I used these sets of cofactors in mqmscan() I got LOD score peaks with different heights with different numbers of cofactors left in the model (ranging from 5 to 20 cofactors).


I suspect that the function mqmautocofactors() involve pseudorandom number generating algorithm because I got the same set of 158 cofactors when I used set.seed() to set the same seed before running mqmautocofactors() function.

My question is how do I report these results? Which LOD profile should I use? Or is it okay if I just randomly pick a seed for mqmautocofactor()?


Many thanks,
Nat

messages.author: 92292fc48bf46044
messages.subject: Re: mqmautocofactors() outputs different sets of cofactors, hence different LOD scores, on different runs
parts:
Deat Nat,

Indeed the autocofactors is a convenience function to place an initial set of cofactors across the genome.
If you get significantly different results, you should build your own genetic cofactors list, and place markers
at locations where you suspect there to be a QTL.

2 approachees:
1) Run different autocofactors runs and build your cofactor list based on which cofactor are not eliminated
2) Another approach I employ is to use scanone and put cofactors at all topmarkers that have a lod score > 2.5, make sure of course that cofactors are not placed within 1 to 2 cM of each other.

Kind regards,
Danny
